meta.title: Power Platform Solution Analyzer
meta.description: Reads a Power Platform estate, says what is technical debt, and estimates what it would cost to fix. Read only. Names what it could not check.
meta.ogDescription: An assessment of a Power Platform estate that never writes to it, and always says what it could not read.
lang.heading: Language
hero.headline: Find out what is actually in there.
hero.lede: It reads a Power Platform estate, tells you what is technical debt and what it would cost to fix, and names every check it could not run. It never writes to the environment.
what.heading: Three moves, in the order a client asks for them.
what.lede: Nobody opens an assessment tool wanting a tool. They want to know what they have, what is wrong with it, and what fixing it costs.
what.card1.title: Counts what is there
what.card1.body: Every component, by type, by solution and by domain. Including a low-code ratio with its definition attached, because the number gets quoted without it.
what.card2.title: Says what is debt
what.card2.body: What Microsoft has removed or deprecated, what was built badly regardless of how it was built, and what nobody would find out about when it breaks. Each one with the evidence that triggered it.
what.card3.title: Puts a number on it
what.card3.body: A range of hours per finding with a rationale, grouped into a backlog somebody would actually groom, adding up to a total whose arithmetic you can check in the room.
modes.heading: Three ways to reach an estate, and what each one gives up.
modes.lede: These are generated from the same contract the product runs on, so this page cannot promise a reach the product does not have.
modes.note: What a mode cannot reach decides which checks can run at all. Every check that could not run is named in the report, with the reason, and is never reported as passing.
modes.summary.servicePrincipal: An Entra app registration added to the environment with a read-only role. The mode for anything repeatable. The role definition ships with the product, so a security team reviews a file rather than a description.
modes.summary.delegated: You, signed in, reading what you can already read. Nothing to create and nothing to approve, which makes it the fastest way to see something real. Not repeatable: a scheduled run cannot borrow your session.
modes.summary.offlineZip: An exported unmanaged solution, read offline. No connection, no credential, no security review. This is the mode that gets past a review in week one while the service principal request sits in a queue.
honesty.heading: It tells you what it could not check.
honesty.body1: Every check declares the evidence it needs. When the way you connected cannot reach that evidence, the check is reported as not assessed, by name, with the reason. It is never reported as passing and never counted as zero findings.
honesty.body2: Telling a client they have no technical debt, when the truth is that nobody could read their environment, is the most damaging thing an assessment can do. So the report carries the list of what it could not check, near the front, where it has to be read.

safety.heading: It cannot change anything in the environment.
safety.body1: Not in any mode, and there is no setting that changes that. A discovery can be run in a first conversation without a change advisory board, which is what makes it usable before anybody has bought anything.
safety.body2: The only thing it writes anywhere is work items into Azure DevOps, Jira or GitHub, and only the ones somebody chose. What it created, where, and when is recorded against the run that did it.
safety.card1.title: Read only, always
safety.card1.body: No mode writes to a Power Platform environment. The least-privilege role definition is a file a client's security team can read before granting anything.
safety.card2.title: No credential in the database
safety.card2.body: Secrets live in Key Vault and are referenced by name. A connection row is therefore safe to read, log and export, which matters because eventually it will be.
safety.card3.title: The publish is narrow
safety.card3.body: Only the items somebody picked on the backlog screen are written, and a dry run shows exactly what would land without writing anything. Every item carries a deterministic key, so publishing twice updates what is there instead of creating a second copy.
safety.card4.title: One client, one engagement
safety.card4.body: Access is per engagement and enforced in the query rather than the screen, so a page that forgets to filter still cannot show one client's estate to another.
output.heading: What leaves the product.
output.lede: Three things, each for a different person in the room, all produced from the stored results of one run rather than from today's rules.
output.card1.title: A findings workbook
output.card1.body: An Excel file with the findings, the inventory, the not-assessed list and the backlog, one sheet each. Deliberately plain, with filters on every header, so an architect can sort and pivot it rather than admire it.
output.card2.title: An assessment report
output.card2.body: A PDF for the person who will not open the workbook. What was read, what was not read, what was found, what it would cost, and where the work sits on a roadmap.
output.card3.title: A groomed backlog
output.card3.body: An epic per category, a feature per rule that needs one, a story per finding worth naming, and the trivia batched. With acceptance criteria, and optionally written straight into Azure DevOps, Jira or GitHub.
rules.heading: {0} categories, counted from the catalogue rather than typed here.
rules.lede: Adding a check updates this page. That is on purpose: a marketing page that claims more than the product does is one somebody eventually reads out loud in a meeting.
rules.note: Some of these come from Microsoft's own Power Apps checker, folded in under Microsoft's rule identifiers so a consultant can look them up. The rest are the ones the checker does not have: lifecycle position, debt spread across components, sprawl and solution hygiene.
rules.categoryBody.lifecycle: Components Microsoft has removed, deprecated or stopped investing in. A dialog still sitting in a solution says more about an estate than any other single component in it.
rules.categoryBody.modernisation: Something that works and has a better answer now. The category a client most wants and the one most easily oversold, so every check here carries a reason to leave the thing alone as well.
rules.categoryBody.quality: How well the thing that exists was built. Error handling, size, naming, structure, and whether a flow that fails does anything about it.
rules.categoryBody.architecture: Whether logic sits where logic should sit. Five different mechanisms firing on one table is a finding even when every one of them works.
rules.categoryBody.alm: Whether this can be moved between environments without somebody remembering something. Hard-coded endpoints, unmanaged customisation in production, components stranded in the default solution.
rules.categoryBody.governance: Ownership, sprawl, orphaned components and premium connector exposure. Including the flows whose owner has left.
rules.categoryBody.performance: Things that are slow now or will be at volume. A synchronous plug-in taking two seconds is what a user means when they say the form hangs.
rules.categoryBody.security: Privilege, secrets in definitions and organisation-level write. Not a penetration test, and it does not pretend to be one.
rules.categoryBody.operability: Whether anybody would find out when it breaks. An estate with no failure alerting anywhere is one where the first report of an outage comes from a customer.
rules.categoryBody.ai: Agents, prompts and models. Whether what the estate has built on AI is grounded in something, current, and owned by somebody.
rules.categoryBody.contactCenter: Workstreams, queues and capacity. Whether a conversation that arrives reaches somebody who can take it -- read only where Contact Center is installed.
languages.heading: Six languages, and three separate settings.
languages.body1: English, Dutch, German, French, Spanish and Italian, throughout: the screens, the rule explanations, the findings, the report and the backlog. The language you read the product in, the language the report comes out in and the language the backlog is written in are three settings, because a Dutch consultant writing an English report for a client's group IT and a Spanish backlog for the delivery team is the normal case rather than an edge one.
limits.heading: What it will not tell you.
limits.lede: A page that only claims is a brochure. These are the questions to take somewhere else.
limits.card1.title: It is not a licensing assessment
limits.card1.body: It reports where a premium connector is used and stops there. It cannot see what the tenant holds, and guessing would be worse than silence.
limits.card2.title: It is not a penetration test
limits.card2.body: The security checks are about privilege, secrets in definitions and organisation-level write. They are not an assessment of whether the estate can be broken into.
limits.card3.title: It does not fix anything
limits.card3.body: There is no remediation mode and no plan to add one. Everything it produces is a recommendation, a report or a work item for somebody who will do the work themselves.
closing.heading: Find out what is actually in there.
closing.body: Sign in with your Microsoft account. A demonstration estate is waiting, with findings the product produced itself, so there is something to look at before a client has given you anything.
privacyPage.title: Privacy — Power Platform Solution Analyzer
privacyPage.description: What this product reads, what it removes, what it refuses to do, and where everything is kept.
privacyPage.heading: What it reads, and what it does not.
privacyPage.lede: Written to be read by a client's security officer rather than by a lawyer. If something here is not clear enough to act on, that is a defect and we would like to hear about it.
privacyPage.reads.heading: What it reads
privacyPage.reads.lede: Only what an assessment needs, and only ever by reading:
privacyPage.reads.item1: Solution and component metadata: which tables, flows, apps, plug-ins, roles and web resources exist, and how they are configured.
privacyPage.reads.item2: The contents of an exported solution file, where one is supplied.
privacyPage.reads.item3: Usage and run history, where the connection reaches it: how often a flow ran, how often it failed, how long a plug-in step took.
privacyPage.reads.item4: The results of Microsoft's Power Apps checker, where it was run.
privacyPage.removed.heading: What it removes
privacyPage.removed.lede: Some things are read in passing and are not kept:
privacyPage.removed.item1: Secrets found inside a definition are counted, never stored and never shown. A finding says that a secret is present and where, not what it is.
privacyPage.removed.item2: Credentials for a connection live in Azure Key Vault and are referenced by name. The product database holds no secret of any kind.
privacyPage.removed.item3: Business data in the tables is not read. The product counts rows; it does not look at them.
privacyPage.refuses.heading: What it refuses to do
privacyPage.refuses.lede: These are not settings. There is no configuration that turns any of them on:
privacyPage.refuses.item1: It never writes to a Power Platform environment, in any mode.
privacyPage.refuses.item2: It never publishes anything to Azure DevOps, Jira or GitHub that somebody did not select, and it never writes to the environment it read.
privacyPage.refuses.item3: It never shows one engagement's estate to somebody who has not been granted access to that engagement.
privacyPage.documents.heading: What goes into the documents
privacyPage.documents.lede: Three things leave the product, and it is worth knowing exactly what is in each:
privacyPage.documents.item1.title: The workbook.
privacyPage.documents.item1.body: Component names, solution names, the findings and their evidence, the estimates and the backlog. Component names are a client's own naming, so treat the file as you would treat their solution export.
privacyPage.documents.item2.title: The report.
privacyPage.documents.item2.body: The same material as narrative, plus the list of what could not be checked. Named components appear where a finding is about one specific thing.
privacyPage.documents.item3.title: The work items.
privacyPage.documents.item3.body: Titles, descriptions and acceptance criteria, written into the client's own Azure DevOps project, Jira project or GitHub repository. Nothing leaves their tenant that was not already in it.
privacyPage.deletion.heading: Deleting an engagement
privacyPage.deletion.body: Deleting an engagement deletes its connections, its runs, its inventory, its findings, its estimates and its backlog, in one operation and without a recycle bin. Work items already published into a client's Azure DevOps, Jira or GitHub are theirs and are not touched.
privacyPage.where.heading: Where it runs
privacyPage.where.body: In Microsoft Azure, in a region chosen for the deployment, in Capgemini's own subscription. The database is reachable only by the product's managed identity; there is no password on it to leak, because there is no password. The one place anything leaves that subscription is Microsoft's own Power Apps checker, where a solution file is analysed in a geography chosen on the connection, and Azure OpenAI, which estimates findings and reads descriptions when a run is set to use a model. That deployment is in the EU data zone and Microsoft does not train models on what is sent to it.
privacyPage.cookies.heading: Cookies on this site
privacyPage.cookies.body: This public site sets one cookie, and only if you press the light and dark switch: it remembers which you chose. There is no analytics, no tracking, no third-party script and no font, image or stylesheet loaded from anywhere that would see you arrive. Signing in sets a session cookie, which is what keeps you signed in.
privacyPage.closing.heading: Still not answered?
privacyPage.closing.body: Ask the team who gave you access. A question that had to be asked usually means this page is missing a paragraph.
